key_insight: Conditioning LLMs on their own past assistant replies is not always beneficial — omitting prior assistant turns (user-turn-only context) can match or improve multi‑turn performance by reducing error propagation and context noise.
problem_solved: Revisits the common design choice of retaining assistant responses in multi‑turn conversation history to determine whether past assistant outputs actually help, or instead introduce errors, cost, and privacy risks.
method: Compare two prompting regimes on in‑the‑wild, multi‑turn conversations: full‑context (includes prior assistant replies) vs user‑turn‑only (omits assistant replies).
Evaluate across three open reasoning models and one state‑of‑the‑art model on metrics such as task accuracy, coherence, hallucination, and instruction adherence.
Run controlled analyses by conversation length and ablation studies to quantify error propagation, latency, and context‑cost tradeoffs.
impact: Findings guide practitioners on conversational system design and prompt strategy: simpler user‑only histories can reduce hallucination, lower compute and privacy exposure, and in many cases improve or preserve performance.
visual_elements: Side‑by‑side conversation schematic: full‑context vs user‑only to show what is included in the prompt.
Bar chart comparing performance metrics (accuracy, hallucination rate, coherence) across prompting regimes and models.
Flow diagram illustrating error propagation when assistant replies are fed back vs interrupted when omitted.
Icon set showing practical benefits: lower API cost, reduced latency, and improved privacy.
paper_title: Do LLMs Benefit From Their Own Words?
paper_authors: Jenny Y. Huang, Leshem Choshen, Ramon Astudillo, Tamara Broderick, Jacob Andreas
